original_value: AbstractObjectiveClinical decision support (CDS) hard-stop alerts—those in which the user is either prevented from taking an action altogether or allowed to proceed only with the external override of a third party—are increasingly common but can be problematic. To understand their appropriate application, we asked 3 key questions: (1) To what extent are hard-stop alerts effective in improving patient health and healthcare delivery outcomes? (2) What are the adverse events and unintended consequences of hard-stop alerts? (3) How do hard-stop alerts compare to soft-stop alerts?Methods and MaterialsStudies evaluating computerized hard-stop alerts in healthcare settings were identified from biomedical and computer science databases, gray literature sites, reference lists, and reviews. Articles were extracted for process outcomes, health outcomes, unintended consequences, user experience, and technical details.ResultsOf 32 studies, 15 evaluated health outcomes, 16 process outcomes only, 10 user experience, and 4 compared hard and soft stops. Seventy-nine percent showed improvement in health outcomes and 88% in process outcomes. Studies reporting good user experience cited heavy user involvement and iterative design. Eleven studies reported on unintended consequences including avoidance of hard-stopped workflow, increased alert frequency, and delay to care. Hard stops were superior to soft stops in 3 of 4 studies.ConclusionsHard stops can be effective and powerful tools in the CDS armamentarium, but they must be implemented judiciously with continuous user feedback informing rapid, iterative design. Investigators must report on associated health outcomes and unintended consequences when implementing IT solutions to clinical problems.

result.paraphrase: AbstractObjectiveClinical decision support (CDS) hard-stop alerts—where users are either completely blocked from acting or can continue only with a third party’s external override—are increasingly common but may be problematic. To assess when they are appropriate, we asked three key questions: (1) How effective are hard-stop alerts at improving patient health and healthcare delivery outcomes? (2) What adverse events and unintended consequences do they cause? (3) How do hard-stop alerts compare with soft-stop alerts?Methods and MaterialsWe identified studies of computerized hard-stop alerts in healthcare settings from biomedical and computer science databases, gray literature sites, reference lists, and reviews. Articles were extracted for process outcomes, health outcomes, unintended consequences, user experience, and technical details.ResultsAmong 32 studies, 15 assessed health outcomes, 16 examined process outcomes only, 10 addressed user experience, and 4 compared hard and soft stops. Seventy-nine percent reported improved health outcomes, and 88% reported improved process outcomes. Studies describing good user experience pointed to strong user involvement and iterative design. Eleven studies reported unintended consequences, including avoidance of hard-stopped workflows, increased alert frequency, and delays in care. Hard stops outperformed soft stops in 3 of 4 studies.ConclusionsHard stops can be effective and powerful tools in the CDS armamentarium, but they must be implemented judiciously with continuous user feedback guiding rapid, iterative design. Researchers should report associated health outcomes and unintended consequences when implementing IT solutions for clinical problems.
